title: Flashing “virus detected” pop-up
setup: You're reading a recipe site on your laptop. Suddenly the screen fills with this, and an alarm starts beeping.

content.subject: WARNING! Your computer is infected
content.body: Trojan spyware detected. Your banking passwords and photos are being stolen. Do NOT close this window or restart your computer.

options.label: Call the number for help
options.feedback: The “technician” charged you for fake repairs and installed remote-access software to get into your bank.

options.label: Close the browser (force quit if needed) and don't call
options.feedback: Real security warnings never include a phone number. Closing the browser ends the scam.

options.label: Click the button to scan your computer
options.feedback: No money gone yet, but “scan” buttons on pages like this can download malware.

redFlags: Real virus warnings never ask you to call a number
Alarms and “do not close” scare tactics
Appeared on a random website
safestAction: Close the browser tab or force quit the browser. If you're worried, run the security software you already have.

title: “Foreign hackers” and a government agent
setup: Yesterday a “tech support” rep helped you remove a pop-up. Today someone calls saying he's from your bank's fraud unit, and a “federal agent” joins the call.

messages.text: The technician you spoke with yesterday found foreign hackers inside your accounts. Your savings are at risk.
I'm transferring you to an agent with the Federal Reserve. They'll open a protected government account so you can move your funds there. Don't tell bank employees — some are involved.

options.label: Move your savings to the “protected” account
options.feedback: There's no such thing as a protected government account. This is a phantom-hacker scam, and the money was gone.

options.label: Hang up and call your bank at the number on your card
options.feedback: Government agencies never ask you to move money, and “don't tell your bank” is a huge red flag.

options.label: Move only half, just to be safe
options.feedback: Half is still going straight to scammers. Any transfer here is a loss.

redFlags: Multiple “officials” working together to seem legit
Told to keep it secret from your bank
The Federal Reserve doesn't hold personal accounts
safestAction: Hang up. Call your bank yourself. No agency will ever ask you to move money or keep secrets from your bank.

title: Buyer asks you to read a code
setup: You posted a bike for sale. A buyer messages right away.

messages.text: Hi! Still available? There are a lot of fake sellers so I want to make sure you're real 🙂
I'm sending a verification code to your phone. Can you tell me the 6 digits?

options.label: Read her the code — seems fair
options.feedback: That code set up an account in your name tied to your phone number, used to scam other people. Or worse, it unlocked one of your accounts.

options.label: Refuse, and don't share any codes
options.feedback: A verification code is a key to an account. Anyone who asks you for one is trying to get in.

options.label: Send her a photo of your ID instead
options.feedback: An ID photo lets scammers open accounts in your name. Never send it to a stranger.

redFlags: Asks for a code sent to your phone
Brand-new profile
“Prove you're real” is the cover story
safestAction: Never share verification codes with anyone. Only type them into the app or site you're logging into yourself.

title: Login code you just requested
setup: You got a new phone and you're signing in to your bank app. The app says it texted you a code.

content.body: Summit Bank: Your one-time code is 482913. It expires in 10 minutes. Don't share this code. We will never call you to ask for it.

options.label: Type the code into the bank app yourself
options.feedback: You requested it, and you're entering it into the app you opened. That's exactly what codes are for.

options.label: Ignore it — codes are a scam
options.feedback: This one you asked for. Codes are only dangerous when someone else asks you to share them.

redFlags: Arrived the moment you requested it
You enter it — you never read it to anyone
Warns you not to share it
safestAction: Use codes only where you requested them. If a code shows up when you didn't ask for one, don't share it with anyone.

title: “Your photos will be deleted” email
setup: You do keep your photos in cloud storage. This email arrives.

content.subject: Payment failed: Your photos will be deleted
content.body:
Dear Customer,

We were unable to renew your storage plan. Your account has exceeded its limit and all photos and videos will be permanently deleted in 48 hours.

Update your payment method now and get 50GB extra free.

options.label: Update your payment so you don't lose your photos
options.feedback: The form sent your card and login to scammers, who also locked you out of your account.

options.label: Open your phone's settings and check your storage plan there
options.feedback: Your real storage status is in your device settings. It showed no problem.

options.label: Unsubscribe using the link at the bottom
options.feedback: No money lost, but links in phishing emails, even unsubscribe links, can lead to fake pages.

redFlags: “Dear Customer” instead of your name
Threat to delete your memories within 48 hours
Sender domain isn't your real provider
safestAction: Don't click. Check your account by opening the app or settings yourself. Report the email as phishing.

title: Security alert after your own login
setup: Five minutes ago you signed in to your email on your new laptop. Then this arrives.

content.subject: New sign-in on MacBook
content.body:
Your account was just signed in to from a new MacBook in Chicago, IL.

If this was you, you don't need to do anything. If not, we'll help you secure your account.
content.footer: You can also review security activity anytime in your account settings.

options.label: It was you. Do nothing, or review activity in your account settings
options.feedback: The alert matches what you just did, it doesn't ask for anything, and checking your settings directly is the gold standard.

options.label: Panic and reset your password using the button in the email
options.feedback: It was real this time, so no harm. But get in the habit of going to your account settings instead of email buttons.

options.label: Reply with your password so they know it's you
options.feedback: No real company wants your password by email. Emailing it put your account at risk.

redFlags: Matches something you did minutes ago
Says “if this was you, do nothing” — no pressure
Points you to your account settings
safestAction: If an alert matches your own activity, you're fine. If it doesn't, go to your account settings directly — not through the email.

title: Fake airline help line in search results
setup: Your flight got canceled. You search “SkyWay Airlines phone number” and tap the top result.

content.subject: Talk to a live SkyWay agent 24/7
content.body: Canceled or delayed flight? Our agents can rebook you instantly. Average wait: under 1 minute.

options.label: Call and let them rebook you with your card
options.feedback: The “agent” charged a rebooking fee and a fake ticket. The airline had no record of it.

options.label: Use the airline's app or the number on your booking confirmation
options.feedback: Sponsored results can be bought by anyone. Your confirmation email and the airline's app have the real contact info.

options.label: Call, but only give your confirmation code
options.feedback: Your confirmation code plus last name can let someone change or cancel your trip.

redFlags: “Sponsored” result, not the airline's own site
Small print: “independent travel assistance”
Domain isn't the airline's real website
safestAction: Get customer-service numbers from the company's app, your receipt, or a website address you type in yourself.

title: CAPTCHA that asks you to run a command
setup: You click a link to download a free PDF. Before the download, a “verify you're human” box appears.

content.subject: Complete these steps to continue
content.body:
1. Press Windows + R
2. Press Ctrl + V
3. Press Enter

This confirms you are not a robot.

options.label: Follow the steps — it's just a CAPTCHA
options.feedback: Those keystrokes ran a hidden command that installed malware. It stole your saved passwords and banking logins.

options.label: Close the page. Real CAPTCHAs never ask you to run commands
options.feedback: Real CAPTCHAs ask you to click boxes or pick pictures — never to press keyboard shortcuts.

options.label: Try it on a different computer instead
options.feedback: Any computer that runs that command gets infected. The trick works the same everywhere.

redFlags: Asks you to press keyboard shortcuts to “verify”
The site copied a command to your clipboard without telling you
Came from a free-download site
safestAction: Close the page. If you already ran the steps, disconnect from the internet, run a security scan, and change your passwords from another device.
